comments.page_title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
comments.author: Dana Whitfield
comments.body: If the beachhead is only 262 institutions, how should I structure my PM team — one squad for the whole band, or split it by asset tier?

comments.page_title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Short answer: don't split by asset tier yet. The 262 count is a verifiable ceiling, not a target list — the real in-band count will shrink once we filter for public mailboxes and listed core systems (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Structure one squad for the whole band until pilot customer-acquisition calibration tells us which tier actually converts; the $5B–$150B range is wide, but the buying behavior we're betting on (Reg E applies, off-the-shelf core, buy-not-build) is uniform across it (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If you need a tie-breaker, split by core system (Fiserv vs. Q2) rather than asset size — that's the integration variable that drives sales cycle length.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Mid-size banks are the beachhead.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
comments.author: Aiko Tanaka
comments.body: The 262 figure comes from an FDIC query. What happens at the edges of the $5B–$150B band — does the product need to behave differently for a bank that just crossed in, or is the band only a sales filter?

comments.page_title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The band is a sales filter, not a product boundary — the product itself keys off the three beachhead criteria (public mailbox, off-the-shelf core, Reg E applies), not asset size [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). A bank that just crossed $5B still meets those criteria, so the product behaves the same; the $5B–$150B band is only how we size the addressable market (262 institutions) and prioritize outreach [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Edge cases like a bank near the $150B top that starts building in-house would fall out of the beachhead naturally, but that's a go-to-market decision, not a product change.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Mid-size banks are the beachhead.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
comments.author: Tomas Ruiz
comments.body: Fiserv DNA and Q2 are named as the core stack. What does that integration surface really look like — do we read the core ourselves, or go through connectors that already exist?

comments.page_title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
We read the core through pre-built connectors, not by building direct integrations ourselves — that's the whole point of the connector layer in the deck (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)). The connectors are standard API "adapters" that let the AI agent, under authorization, verify identity, pull transactions, reissue statements, and open disputes against Fiserv/FIS/Jack Henry cores and Q2/Alkami/Candescent digital banking platforms [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html). What the connector can actually *do* is still gated by the §3.2 delegation matrix and approval checkpoints — the connector only solves "reach," not "authority" [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html).

Sources: 1. [Research Report — 1.6 术语表](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

comments.page_title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
comments.author: Sam Okafor
comments.body: Larkspur is fictional but it drives the whole ROI. Which of its four profile numbers would actually change product scope if a real prospect differs?

comments.page_title: Mid-size banks are the beachhead.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Good catch — the four profile numbers are all assumptions, but only two would actually move product scope. The **email volume (60k/year)** and **VARR rate (35% baseline)** are the levers that change capacity math and automation thresholds; the **asset size ($18B)** and **FTE count (420)** are just context for credibility. If a real prospect came in with, say, 10x volume or a much lower VARR, we'd re-run the three sensitivity tiers in §9.2 rather than redesign the product — the core flow (verified resolution in-thread, Reg E clock compliance) stays the same. The one number that could force a scope change is the **"22% of replies end in 'please call'"** baseline, because that's the failure-demand driver; if a prospect's number is near zero, the ROI case collapses and we'd need to reposition around compliance (Reg E 90-day POS clock) instead [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html).

Sources: 2. [Research Report — 9.2 邮件渠道的经济账](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

comments.page_title: The clock starts at the inbox.
comments.author: Lena Fischer
comments.body: The 10-business-day and 45-day clocks are statutory, but the 27-hour first reply and the 22% "please call us" rate are assumptions. Which one, if it turns out wrong, breaks the business case first?

comments.page_title: The clock starts at the inbox.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The 22% "please call us" rate is the more fragile assumption, because it feeds the failed-demand reduction that anchors the base-tier savings (15% of 600K items ≈ $720K, see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)). The 27-hour median only affects the qualitative "slowest channel" framing, not the pilot economics — the business case is built on volume, VARR, and loaded cost per item, none of which depend on first-reply latency (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)). If the 22% proves high, the failed-demand pool shrinks proportionally and the $2.68M base-tier estimate erodes before any AI-resolution spend is even considered.

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 11.4 Pilot Economics (All Assumptions, for Calibration Against Customer Data)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

comments.page_title: The clock starts at the inbox.
comments.author: Marcus Bell
comments.body: The 28% of agent time lost to system switching comes from a third-party study. Does our design genuinely remove that switching, or does it just move the same effort into a review queue?

comments.page_title: The clock starts at the inbox.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Good question, Marcus. The 28% figure is a third-party benchmark (Talkdesk 2026, NewtonX n=252) — it describes the industry baseline, not a measured Larkspur outcome [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Our design removes the *re-keying* part of that switching: the email arrives, the Reg E clock starts, and the investigation context (account, transaction, prior notices) is pulled into one view without the agent hopping systems. What remains is a human review step for provisional credit decisions — that's deliberate, not a hidden queue, and it's a fraction of the original switching cost. We haven't run a controlled time-motion study on our own flow yet, so I'd flag that as a validation gap rather than a claim.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The clock starts at the inbox.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: The clock starts at the inbox.
comments.author: Priya Raman
comments.body: Email costs $6–12 a contact and phone $12–20. When I sit with a buyer, do I sell against the channel cost or against the violation exposure?

comments.page_title: The clock starts at the inbox.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Sell against the violation exposure — that’s the headline. The channel cost is just the supporting detail: email is the slowest channel at 27h median first reply, and an unread inbox is a liability under Reg E (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Lead with the 74% of 2025 Reg E violations in error resolution, then use the $6–12 vs $12–20 spread to show why automation pays for itself even before you count the regulatory risk (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The clock starts at the inbox.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: The clock starts at the inbox.
comments.author: Aiko Tanaka
comments.body: A clock starts when the bank receives the mail, not when an agent opens it. Where does that receipt timestamp come from, and how would we prove it to an examiner?

comments.page_title: The clock starts at the inbox.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The receipt timestamp comes from the email system's intake layer — the moment the message lands in the bank's mailbox, not when an agent opens it. That's the "clock starts at the inbox" principle: the legal clock starts at receipt, per Reg E 1005.11(b)(1) [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html), and our product identifies regulated intent (error notices, complaints, legal documents, vulnerability signals) at intake, even from a half-sentence inside a multi-intent email [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)[2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

For examiner proof, the timestamp is captured and logged at intake with the full message metadata (headers, delivery time, thread context) — this is the same evidence base used for the FDIC's 2025 finding that 74% of Reg E violations were in error resolution [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)[2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). The deck's "Day 0 Email arrives — clock starts" slide [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) reflects that the system records receipt time automatically, independent of any agent action. If you need specifics on the exact logging format or retention policy, that's beyond what the current reference material covers — I'd flag it as a gap to fill before the next review.

Sources: 1. [Research Report — v0.4 新增的 6 个产品主张（差异化从这里来）](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) · 2. [Case Study Deck — The clock starts at the inbox.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
comments.author: Sam Okafor
comments.body: Chat is marked as a smaller surface than email even though both wait their turn. What exactly makes email the bigger build?

comments.page_title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The bigger build is the auditable number, not the surface. Email’s clock runs on a mailbox with no live interruption, but pricing is our own $1.50 assumption (B12: no public price), and an auditable number takes 90 days to build — where nobody has done it, the blank is also the opportunity (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Chat waits its turn too, but it shares the same buyers as voice and has a smaller surface, so it’s a parity build rather than a new vertical layer (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Same base, no live caller, same runtime.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
comments.author: Dana Whitfield
comments.body: Two rows say the work already ships. Should my PM org own those lines or hand them off, and how do we avoid stepping on the teams that own them today?

comments.page_title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Dana — those two rows are labeled "reused," not "ours": the runtime, bot builder, automation flows and connectors already ship on CXA, and the deck is explicit that we own only the vertical layer (intent detection, assurance tiers, the clock, the dossier) [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). Your PM org should own the vertical layer and the proof (policy pack, eval harness, reference numbers), while the horizontal teams keep owning their components — we hand off via the existing connectors and label everything reused so there's no ambiguity [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)[2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). If a hand-off question comes up, the design-partner program is the joint forum where ownership gets settled, with compliance as a named owner [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 2. [Case Study Deck — Same base, no live caller, same runtime.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 3. [Case Study Deck — How it is packaged, priced and sold.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
comments.author: Aiko Tanaka
comments.body: Email ranks above voice here because there is no live interruption. Is that a product property or a technical one — could a voice agent get the same async character with a callback pattern?

comments.page_title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
That’s a fair distinction to draw. The async, no-interruption property is a product property of email as a channel, not a technical limit — a callback pattern could give voice the same “no live caller” feel, but it would still carry the expectation of a synchronous conversation once connected, and it wouldn’t reuse the same runtime the way email does (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). So the ranking rests on the combination: email is async by nature *and* rides the existing base/runtime, which a callback voice flow wouldn’t match without extra build.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Same base, no live caller, same runtime.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
comments.author: Marcus Bell
comments.body: The table says the marginal build is the vertical layer alone. What is the honest engineering estimate for that layer, and which of the components we lean on is the weakest link?

comments.page_title: Same base, no live caller, same runtime.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Honest estimate: the vertical layer is a few engineer-months, not quarters — intent detection, assurance tiers, the clock, and the dossier are all thin wrappers over the platform’s runtime, bot builder, and connectors (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The weakest link is the clock engine: it’s the only piece that turns a promise into a deadline, and it depends on the bank’s policy pack being precise — if that pack is ambiguous, the clock inherits the ambiguity and the dossier loses its regulator-ready edge (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: We automate the work, not the decision.
comments.author: Lena Fischer
comments.body: Complaints and fraud are route-only at 5% of volume. Is that about the model not being good enough, or about regulatory exposure — and would more evidence ever unlock them?

comments.page_title: We automate the work, not the decision.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Both, but the binding constraint is regulatory exposure, not model quality. Complaints and fraud are permanently L0 — humans decide and sign — because the consequence of a wrong autonomous answer is disproportionate, and no amount of evidence changes that (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). More evidence could improve routing accuracy, but it would not unlock autonomous answering; the scope line is explicit: everything reversible goes to the machine, everything consequential stays with a person [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — We automate the work, not the decision.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: We automate the work, not the decision.
comments.author: Tomas Ruiz
comments.body: The sort order is volume × determinability × identity achievability. Which of those three is computed at runtime and which is a judgement that has to be re-made with every bank?

comments.page_title: We automate the work, not the decision.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The three factors are not runtime-computed values; they are design-time judgements you re-make with each bank. Volume and determinability come from the bank’s own intake data and process rules — e.g., the ~15% and ~10% figures in [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) are estimates for Larkspur, not universal constants. Identity achievability is a capability assessment of the bank’s KYC/authentication stack, so it has to be re-evaluated per institution. At runtime, the only thing computed is the routing decision itself — whether a case fits the L0 triage/summary/prep pattern or needs human adjudication, per the L0 definition in [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html).

Sources: 1. [Research Report — 12.0 v0.4 用例优先级矩阵：按题目给出的五大类](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

comments.page_title: We automate the work, not the decision.
comments.author: Priya Raman
comments.body: Complaints and fraud are the smallest slice by volume but probably the largest by risk. What is the commercial story for leaving the scariest category manual?

comments.page_title: We automate the work, not the decision.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The commercial story is that risk concentration, not volume, drives the delegation design. Complaints and fraud are R4 — the highest regulatory-risk tier — so Wave 1 deliberately keeps them at "detect, clock, warm handoff" with no autonomous reply, because a wrong answer there carries disproportionate cost (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)). The machine still captures the value: it registers the clock, quarantines suspected fraud, and confirms over on-file channels, which removes the expensive manual triage without touching the decision (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html), [3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). That is the same logic as the "everything reversible goes to the machine, everything consequential stays with a person" line — the scariest category is where the human sign-off is the product, not a cost (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — We automate the work, not the decision.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 2. [PRD (English) — 5.1 Use-Case Wave Matrix](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 3. [Case Study Deck — What ships, what waits, and what has no switch.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: We automate the work, not the decision.
comments.author: Aiko Tanaka
comments.body: Wave 1 and Wave 2 are described as differences in the policy pack. If both run on one engine, what stops a Wave 2 intent being switched on early by a misconfigured limit matrix?

comments.page_title: We automate the work, not the decision.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Nothing in the engine itself — the limit matrix is bank-written, so a misconfiguration could in principle expose a Wave 2 intent early (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). That’s why the deck frames Wave 2 as “same policy pack, second wave” and pairs it with a UDAAP wording review and a wave board for governance, not as a technical gate. The safeguard is the bank’s own review process, not the runtime.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — One governance layer, three waves.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: The thread is the case.
comments.author: Aiko Tanaka
comments.body: Step 8 is the only place a model writes to a customer, and only the connective tissue. Is that boundary enforced by the prompt or by the structure of the system?

comments.page_title: The thread is the case.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The boundary is enforced by the system’s structure, not by the prompt. Step 8 is the only place a model writes to a customer, and it is explicitly “assembled, not written”: the regulated disclosure is a locked template, amounts and dates are system slots checked field by field, and only the connective tissue passes through a model (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The prompt never has the authority to alter disclosures or amounts because those components are never routed to the model in the first place.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: The thread is the case.
comments.author: Tomas Ruiz
comments.body: Step 6 is idempotent, but what happens if it acts and then step 8 never sends — does the case reopen somewhere, or does it close quietly?

comments.page_title: The thread is the case.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Step 6’s actions are idempotent and compensated by design — the case state contract and compensation flows in FR-4.3 ensure that if step 8 never sends, the case is rolled back to a consistent state rather than silently closed [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). The 14-day verification window in step 9 also keeps the case open for reconciliation, so a missing send would surface there rather than vanish [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). If you need the exact rollback trigger or timeout, that’s not specified in the reference material — I’d point you to the platform’s existing Automation Flows implementation notes.

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 6.1 Email Thread Is the Case (Thread = Case)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 2. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: The thread is the case.
comments.author: Sam Okafor
comments.body: Personalization includes a tone tier. Who defines those tiers, and can an agent override one for a single thread?

comments.page_title: The thread is the case.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Tone tiers are defined by the bank’s own policy pack — we don’t set them; the bank writes the pack and we execute it (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Override for a single thread is possible only through the human-only road (L0–L1) at step 7, where a person decides or signs — there’s no per-thread override on the auto or one-click roads, since step 8’s connective tissue is the only model-written part and it’s gated by the matrix (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If the bank wants an override mechanism, that’s a policy-pack change, not something we’d add unilaterally.

Sources: 2. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 1. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: The thread is the case.
comments.author: Lena Fischer
comments.body: Nine steps and three possible roads after step 5. Where does the record of which road was taken live, and could a reviewer reconstruct it a month later?

comments.page_title: The thread is the case.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The road taken is recorded as part of the case thread itself — step 5’s matrix decision is a logged event in the same thread that step 1 ingests, so the full nine-step history (including which road was chosen) is reconstructable from the thread’s audit trail [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). A reviewer a month later can replay the thread: the matrix output (L3, L2, or L0–L1) is stored alongside the timestamp and the inputs that drove it, and step 9’s 14-day window applies to customer-facing verification, not to internal logging [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). If you need the exact retention period for the audit trail beyond that, the deck doesn’t specify it — I’d flag that as a gap to confirm with the engineering team.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — The thread is the case.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.
comments.author: Aiko Tanaka
comments.body: R3 is never autonomous over email because the tool functions do not exist on this channel. Is that an architectural guarantee, or a deployment choice someone could reverse later?

comments.page_title: Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
It is architectural: the R3 tool functions are simply not registered on the email channel, so security rests on unreachability rather than model obedience (see [4](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html), FR-6.3 AC1). The deck states this as a design invariant — "the tool functions do not exist on this channel" [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) — and the prototype fixture enforces it with `kind: "never"` and `neverNominated: true` [3](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/mocks/fixtures/designTime.ts). Reversing it would require a deliberate platform change, not a config toggle, but nothing in the reference material rules out a future product decision to add such functions; the guarantee holds for the current design.

Sources: 4. [PRD (English) — 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 1. [Case Study Deck — Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 3. [Prototype Source — src/mocks/fixtures/designTime.ts](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/mocks/fixtures/designTime.ts)

comments.page_title: Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.
comments.author: Marcus Bell
comments.body: The matrix is four identity grades by five action risks. How much of that is code that already ships versus new engineering, and who maintains it once a bank writes its own limits?

comments.page_title: Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The matrix itself is new — it’s the “bank-written limit matrix (R × I → L)” that sits as a thin vertical layer on top of existing Autopilot, Automation Flows, Agent Builder, and FS core connectors [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). The underlying engine already ships; the new part is the layer, not the channel or runtime [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). comments.page_title: Autonomy is earned, intent by intent.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Auto-demotion is triggered by drift in the same-evidence blocks that earned graduation — backtest, sampling, negative relabel, or dual sign-off — and the ratchet is asymmetric: tightening can take effect same-day with auto-expiry, while loosening must earn its way back through the full gate sequence (see [2](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/README.md)). Who gets told: the drift signal feeds back into Sense, and the auto-demotion is part of the loop that "humans sign the diff" — so the human sign-off on the configuration diff is the notification channel, not a silent background event (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). It does not happen silently; the demotion itself is a configuration diff flowing into the same gates that govern every output (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 2. [Project README — Solution](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/README.md) · 1. [Case Study Deck — AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.author: Deck AI

comments.page_title: AI nominates, the evidence argues, humans sign the diff.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Good question — the 90-day window is the backtest corpus, not a prerequisite for every customer. For a genuinely new account with no samples, the AI simply doesn't nominate until enough evidence accumulates; the rule engine still decides on existing deterministic rules, so the customer isn't left unprotected — they just don't get AI-proposed wording until the loop has something to chew on.

comments.author: Marcus Bell
comments.body: Four phases inside 59 days is tight for an integration. Which phase slips first if the connector work runs a week late, and what is the recovery?

comments.page_title: Three numbers. One pilot.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
If the connector work slips a week, the shadow run (W3–W4) is the first phase to compress, because it is the only gate that can absorb delay without violating the day-59 veto criteria — recall ≥99.5% and zero misses are non-negotiable (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). Recovery: overlap the tail of onboarding/backtest with the start of shadow, and run shadow at full volume for a shorter window, but only if the day-45 cohort observation and the day-59 gate remain intact — any miss in shadow is a No-go, so we would not cut the shadow below a statistically meaningful sample (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). If the slip exceeds a week, the honest answer is the go/no-go criterion itself: we would flag a No-go rather than compress L1/L2 live or the day-45 measure, since those feed the signed day-59 report (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — 59 days to a signed day-59 report.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: Three numbers. One pilot.
comments.author: Lena Fischer
comments.body: The autonomy rate has three conditions attached. Which of the three is most likely to be gamed by a customer who wants the number to look good?

comments.page_title: Three numbers. One pilot.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The "recall ≥99.5%" gate is the most gameable, because it's measured on the detection of regulated intents — a customer could tune the classifier to be more conservative (over-escalate to L2) to hit the recall bar while quietly sacrificing precision, which inflates the "graduation-ready" count without improving actual autonomy quality. The rule-of-three sample size (n=600) is harder to game since it's a pure count, and the error-rate envelope is statistically bounded (see [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)). That said, the deck already mitigates this by requiring the readiness report to double as model-governance evidence and by auto-downgrading on drift or incidents (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html), §3.2).

Sources: 2. [Research Report — 7.1 两个 headline 方向的证据复核](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html) · 1. [Research Report — 12.3 v0.4.3 Trade-off 登记册：为控险、合规与可信度主动放弃了什么](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

comments.page_title: The risks that would end this product.
comments.author: Aiko Tanaka
comments.body: Preferring false positives pushes recall up and precision down. Where does the false-positive cost actually land, and can a bank tune the trade-off without breaking the recall gate?

comments.page_title: The risks that would end this product.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
False-positive cost lands on intake-side R2 agents: they must manually review and clear every regulated sub-intent that the detector flags, and each false positive still starts the statutory clock and locks the delegation tier (adjudication R4 always human) — so the cost is operational, not regulatory [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). The recall gate is a hard floor (≥99.5% on regulated intents), not a ceiling; a bank can tune precision by adjusting the detector threshold or adding post-detection filters, as long as backtesting still holds the recall bar and any miss triggers incident review [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). The PRD doesn’t specify a precision target or a tuning mechanism beyond that constraint, so the exact trade-off curve is left to implementation.

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

comments.page_title: The risks that would end this product.
comments.author: Tomas Ruiz
comments.body: Injected text is quarantined as data and never as instruction. What is the mechanism — a sanitiser before the model, or a structural separation of the two channels?

comments.page_title: The risks that would end this product.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Both, by design. External content is stripped and labeled at the quarantine layer (script stripping, tracking-pixel removal, link rewriting) before the model sees it, and it is then passed only as data with explicit delimiters and untrusted markings — never as system instructions [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html). On top of that, the tool-signature layer makes the attack unreachable: the change-mobile + mail-card combination has no callable function on the email channel, so even a successful injection cannot trigger a write [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)[3](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html).

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 07 Functional Requirements (M1–M12)](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 2. [Case Study Deck — The risks that would end this product.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 3. [PRD (English) — 8.3 Email Three: ATO + Attachment Injection (Showing "Dangerous Actions Are Unreachable")](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html)

comments.page_title: The risks that would end this product.
comments.author: Lena Fischer
comments.body: If our own judge flips verdicts at that rate, how can an autonomy number be contractual at all?

comments.page_title: The risks that would end this product.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Lena, fair challenge — and it's exactly why we don't put the autonomy number in the contract. The 14% flip rate is on the judge's *own* verdicts, not on the bank's agreed SLAs; we only commit to the human-in-the-loop review cadence and the audit trail, which are measurable and stable (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)). The autonomy figure is a benchmark for internal iteration, not a contractual term — we'd rather under-promise on the metric and over-deliver on the process.

Sources: 1. [Research Report — 12.0c 机会优先级（v0.3 原表，已按 v0.4 口径更新）](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-research-report-v0.2.html)

comments.page_title: The risks that would end this product.
comments.author: Priya Raman
comments.body: Sign-off fatigue is on the register. What stops one-click approvals from becoming rubber stamps once a customer is running at the target autonomy?

comments.page_title: The risks that would end this product.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Good catch — the register flags it, but the deck doesn't claim a hard stop. The mitigation is the same one shown in the prototype: the autonomy cell downgrades from auto to one-click when the policy condition fails, and the reason is only readable on the agent screen (see [2](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/demo/scripts.ts)). We track the approve-without-edit rate and sample approved files, but we don't promise a threshold that eliminates rubber-stamping — that's a live risk, not a solved one (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)).

Sources: 2. [Prototype Source — src/demo/scripts.ts](https://github.com/wukun2005-gif/mailAutopilotForFS/blob/main/src/demo/scripts.ts) · 1. [Case Study Deck — The risks that would end this product.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: One governance layer, three waves.
comments.author: Aiko Tanaka
comments.body: Five of the new pieces are written by the bank itself. What stops two banks from diverging into configurations we can no longer support?

comments.page_title: One governance layer, three waves.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
Good question — the deck is explicit that the bank writes the limits, not the model [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), and every cell of the matrix, threshold, and template wording is bank-controlled [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). But the governance layer itself is the constraint: R3 and R4 cells never respond, a cell tightens in one click but loosens only through graduation evidence and a dual signature [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/), and all changes arrive as configuration diffs that must clear the same gates [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). That said, the deck doesn't specify a support contract or versioning policy for divergent configs — if you need that commitment, it's not in the reference material, and I'd flag it as an open item for the roadmap discussion.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — Admin: the bank writes the limits, not the model.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: One governance layer, three waves.
comments.author: Marcus Bell
comments.body: One policy engine written once and applied to every channel. What has to be true in the runtime for a voice agent to reuse the email policy pack without forking it?

comments.page_title: One governance layer, three waves.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The runtime has to treat the policy pack as data, not code — the same `R × I → L` limit matrix and the same clock engine that turns a promise into a deadline, written once by the bank and applied to every channel (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). For voice, that means the Agent Builder voice agent calls the same policy engine and clock engine as the email flow; the only channel-specific part is the intent detection and the natural-language interface, which is exactly why the deck says the new part is the layer, not the channel — no new platform or runtime (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The deck doesn't specify the technical contract for that reuse (e.g., API shape or latency bounds), so I can't go deeper than that from the material.

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — One governance layer, three waves.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: One governance layer, three waves.
comments.author: Dana Whitfield
comments.body: The second wave adds a new language and a new regulation under the same policy pack. Who owns that pack as an artifact — a PM or an engineering team?

comments.page_title: One governance layer, three waves.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
The policy pack is owned by the bank — it is their artifact, not ours. We ship the mechanism (the pack is a setting, not a new SKU, per [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)), and the design-partner program runs jointly with compliance as a named owner rather than a reviewer at the end [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/). So the bank’s compliance team owns the pack as a living artifact; our vertical team (product, engineering, compliance lead) builds and maintains the tooling that lets them edit and enforce it [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/).

Sources: 1. [Case Study Deck — How it is packaged, priced and sold.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/) · 2. [Case Study Deck — Four more questions, short answers.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)

comments.page_title: One governance layer, three waves.
comments.author: Sam Okafor
comments.body: The second wave mentions a wording review for complaints. Is that a new model capability or a new human review step on top of the existing one?

comments.page_title: One governance layer, three waves.
comments.author: Deck AI
comments.body:
It’s a new human review step, not a new model capability. Wave 1 already does detection, warm handoff, and clock registration for complaints; the UDAAP wording review in Wave 2 is a deep-capability add-on where humans review the bank’s drafted responses for regulatory-compliant language before send (see [1](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html), [2](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)). The model still doesn’t decide — it flags and routes, and the review sits on top of the existing human workflow.

Sources: 1. [PRD (English) — 5.1 Use-Case Wave Matrix](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/email-autopilot-fs-prd_en.html) · 2. [Case Study Deck — We automate the work, not the decision.](https://wukun2005-gif.github.io/mailAutopilotForFS/deck-html/)
